---
title: "📉 CMSY++ catch-only stock assessment"
description: >
  cmsy_area(), cmsy_system(), cmsy_setup(), cmsy_priors(), cmsy_input(), cmsy_run(), cmsy_plot(), cmsy_forecast(), cmsy_compare() and cmsy_tables(): catch-only assessments of FAO catch series with the bundled CMSY++ code, FishBase priors and JAGS.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
FAO34 <- suppressMessages(fishing_area_data("Atlantic, Eastern Central", plot = FALSE))
# Charts made beforehand by data-raw/cmsy_article_figures.R (JAGS is not available when the site is built)
fig_dir <- normalizePath(file.path("figures", "cmsy", "en"))
show_png <- function(file) {
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf('<figure class="fao-figure"><img src="%s" alt="%s" loading="lazy"></figure>',
                             knitr::image_uri(file.path(fig_dir, file)), file))
}
```

CMSY++ (Froese et al. 2023) estimates MSY, Bmsy and Fmsy, and the relative stock size (B/Bmsy) and exploitation (F/Fmsy) of every year, from a catch series, a prior for the intrinsic growth rate r and priors for the relative biomass B/k. The package bundles the official CMSY++ code (`CMSY++16.R`, January 2021), its neural network and its user guide, and a few functions take care of everything from installing JAGS to drawing the charts.

::: {.alert .alert-warning}
**FishStat has catches only, no CPUE.** The FAO capture statistics have no abundance index (CPUE or survey biomass), so every stock is assessed with the catch-only part of CMSY++ (CMSY, `btype = "None"`) and the Bayesian Schaefer model (BSM) does not run. The results then depend mostly on the B/k priors, and independent tests found that catch-only methods classify stock status poorly with default priors (Free et al. 2020; Ovando et al. 2021; Kell et al. 2022). The results are **indicative** and do not replace stock assessments. As in FAO (2026), the status has two classes only: **maximally sustainably fished** (B/Bmsy at least 0.8 in the last year) or **overfished** (below 0.8); catch-only results do not make a stock "underfished".
:::

## 🚀 One step: cmsy_area()

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cmsy_setup()                                                     # once: JAGS and the R packages
area34 <- cmsy_area("Atlantic, Eastern Central", top = 10)
```

`cmsy_area()` does Steps 1 to 9 below in one call: it takes the `top` species with the largest catch of the last `recent_years` years (10 by default) of a fishing area (or the species given in `species`), prepares the input, runs CMSY++, draws all charts, projects the stocks and writes the tables, with a progress bar for each step. `area` can name several areas; each gets its own folder in `out_dir` (`cmsy_areas` by default), sorted into:

```
cmsy_areas/Atlantic__Eastern_Central/
├── input/      CMSY++ catch and ID files, the stocks assessed, and main species left out with the reason
├── runs/       CMSY++ output of each stock (JPEG charts, cmsy_output.csv, log.txt), changed code and list of changes
├── figures/    a folder of charts per stock and summary/ (figures_pptx/ with pptx = TRUE)
└── tables/     results.csv, series.csv, priors and results tables, projections and sources.csv
```

On a Mac with Apple silicon, the six main species of area 34 take about a minute from input to tables.

## 💻 Step 1: check the computer and adapt the settings

The CMSY++ code was written on Windows. Its user guide (step 12) tells Mac users to change every `windows()` to `quartz()` and `antialias = "cleartype"` to `"default"`. The code tests for Windows with `grepl("win", sysname)`, which is also true for macOS ("Darwin"), so on a Mac it calls `windows()` and stops. `cmsy_system()` finds the operating system, R version, processor, JAGS and R packages, and shows the settings `cmsy_run()` will use:

```{r}
sys <- cmsy_system()
show_table(sys$changes)
```

The changes are made to a copy of the code written into each run folder (`CMSY++16_faofishingreport.R`, with the list in `code_changes.csv`); the bundled original never changes. Charts are drawn on an off-screen device by default, which saves the JPEG files on every system without opening windows; `device = "screen"` uses the system's own window instead. If the detection is wrong, set the system:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cmsy_system(os = "windows")                       # settings used on Windows
options(faofishingreport.cmsy_os = "macos")       # for the whole session
```

## 🧰 Step 2: install JAGS and the R packages

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cmsy_setup()
```

`cmsy_setup()` asks before installing anything. It installs the missing R packages from CRAN (R2jags, rjags, coda, gplots, mvtnorm, neuralnet, conicfit; snpar, archived on CRAN on 2022-05-10, is replaced by the same runs test), downloads the JAGS installer for the system and R version from its pinned link, checks its size and MD5 checksum and opens it (`.exe` on Windows, `.pkg` on macOS; on Linux it downloads the source and shows the commands), and checks the bundled CMSY++ files. Restart R after installing JAGS and run `cmsy_setup()` again.

JAGS 4.3.2 (4.3.1 for older R versions) is the default because rjags on CRAN (4-17) needs JAGS 4. The newest JAGS, 5.0.0, needs rjags 5-3 from SourceForge: `cmsy_setup(jags = "latest")`. Installers copied into `inst/jags/` of the package source are used instead of downloading. Versions, links, sizes, checksums, licences and references of every component:

```{r}
src <- cmsy_sources()
show_table(src[, c("component", "version", "platform", "file", "license", "url")], n = 30)
```

### The R version and the JAGS version must match

JAGS is a separate program that rjags uses for the MCMC. On Windows and macOS each JAGS installer is built for a range of R versions; with the wrong one rjags cannot be loaded and CMSY++ cannot run. rjags on CRAN (4-17) needs JAGS 4. The matches (JAGS 4 is the default):

| System | R version | JAGS installer | rjags |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows | 4.5, 4.6 | `JAGS-4.3.2.exe` | 4-17 (CRAN) |
| Windows | 4.2 to 4.4 | `JAGS-4.3.1.exe` | 4-17 (CRAN) |
| macOS | 4.3 and later | `JAGS-4.3.2.pkg` | 4-17 (CRAN) |
| macOS | 4.2 | `JAGS-4.3.1.pkg` | 4-17 (CRAN) |
| Linux | any | the system package (e.g. `sudo apt-get install jags`) or `JAGS-4.3.2.tar.gz` | 4-17 (CRAN, built from source) |
| Windows | 4.5, 4.6 | `JAGS-5.0.0.exe` (optional, newest) | 5-3 (SourceForge, not yet on CRAN) |
| macOS | 4.3 and later | `JAGS-5.0.0-universal.pkg` (optional) | 5-3 (SourceForge: binary for R 4.6, else from source) |

The rules come from the README of the JAGS downloads (e.g. the Windows build of JAGS 4.3.2 "was built with Rtools45 and is suitable for interfacing with R 4.5.x"; "JAGS-4.3.2.pkg for compatibility with R version 4.3.0 and later"; "JAGS-4.3.1.pkg for compatibility with R versions 4.0.x to 4.2.x"), and each combination is installed and run with CMSY++ by the package's GitHub Actions workflow. `cmsy_jags_versions()` gives the table, marks the row for this computer and gives the evidence and README link of each rule:

```{r}
jv <- cmsy_jags_versions()
show_table(jv[, c("system", "r_versions", "jags", "installer", "rjags", "default", "this_computer")], n = 10)
```

No need to look it up: `cmsy_download_jags()` picks the installer for the system, R version and processor, downloads it and checks its size, MD5 and SHA-256; for JAGS 5 it also downloads rjags 5-3. It can also download for other systems or R versions, e.g. to prepare installers for computers without internet:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cmsy_download_jags()                                        # the JAGS for this computer
cmsy_download_jags(version = "latest")                      # JAGS 5.0.0 and rjags 5-3
cmsy_download_jags(os = "all", r_version = "4.4.1", dest = "jags_installers")   # all systems, R 4.4
cmsy_install_jags()                                         # download and open the installer
```

## 🐟 Step 3: priors for r from FishBase and SeaLifeBase

A built-in table gives the resilience and prior r of the 3,155 species-level items of the FAO capture statistics in FishBase or SeaLifeBase (release 26.06). It can be searched offline by English, Chinese or scientific name or by 3-alpha code, and every row links to its source page (`open = TRUE` opens the pages):

```{r}
cod <- cmsy_priors("Gadus morhua")
show_table(cod[, c("species_name", "scientific_name", "SpecCode", "resilience", "prior_r",
                   "r_low", "r_high", "r_source", "url")])
```

The r range follows the CMSY++ user guide: the 95% confidence limits of FishBase's prior r when the species has one (user guide Table 1, "alternatively and better"); otherwise the range of its resilience (Table 2: High 0.6–1.5, Medium 0.2–0.8, Low 0.05–0.5, Very low 0.015–0.1); otherwise none, and the user gives it (e.g. r close to 2M or 2Fmsy, Table 1). FAO names are matched as valid species names, then through each database's own synonym table; ambiguous synonyms and genus or family items get no values.

```{r}
priors <- cmsy_priors()
table(priors$match_type)
```

Species can be named by English or Chinese FAO name, both together (as shown with `lang = "both"`), scientific name or FAO 3-alpha code, in `cmsy_priors()`, `cmsy_input(species = )`, `cmsy_run(stocks = )` and `cmsy_plot(stocks = )`: full names are matched first (ignoring case), then parts of names; if several species match, they are listed so a more precise name or code can be given. `lang` sets the language of the results; `species_en` and `species_zh` always give both names.

```{r}
p <- cmsy_priors(c("COD", "Sardina pilchardus", "European pilchard"), lang = "both")
show_table(p[, c("species_name", "scientific_name", "alpha3", "r_low", "r_high", "url", "data_url", "rule_url")])
```

Every row links to its sources: `url`, the FishBase or SeaLifeBase page of the species (where resilience and prior r can be checked); `data_url`, the FishBase or SeaLifeBase table the value was read from (`estimate` for prior r, `stocks` for resilience); and `rule_url`, the CMSY++ user guide, whose Tables 1 and 2 turn the values into the r range. The results of `cmsy_input()` and `cmsy_run()` add `fao_data_url`, the FAO data release used.

## 🧾 Step 4: FAO data to CMSY++ input files

```{r}
input <- cmsy_input(FAO34$area_data)
input
table(input$excluded$reason)
```

A stock is the catch of one species item in one fishing area summed over countries (`by = "country"` keeps countries apart); only items identified to species and measured in tonnes are used. Following the user guide, years are consecutive: a stock runs from its first to its last year with catch, and missing or zero years in between are interpolated (and counted). Stocks are left out with fewer than `min_years` years (default 10: CMSY++ uses the first and last ten years for its default priors), less than `min_catch` tonnes, more than `max_filled` years filled (default 20%) or no r prior. Expert priors replace the defaults:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
input <- cmsy_input(FAO34$area_data,
                    priors = data.frame(alpha3 = "PIL", endb.low = 0.2, endb.hi = 0.6))
```

## ▶️ Step 5: run CMSY++

```{r, eval = FALSE}
result <- cmsy_run(input, stocks = "Brachydeuterus auritus", auto_start = TRUE, seed = 1,
                   plots = c("analysis", "management", "kobe", "prior_posterior", "retrospective"))
result$summary
```

`stocks` takes `Stock` identifiers (e.g. `"GRB_34"`) or species by English or Chinese name, scientific name or 3-alpha code (all stocks of the species). Each stock runs in its own folder, `cmsy/<area>/<stock>/`, and R process; the folders keep CMSY++'s own output (`_AN.jpg`, `_MAN.jpg`, `_KOBE.jpg`, `cmsy_output.csv`, `log.txt`). `parallel` sets how many stocks run at the same time, and a progress bar shows the stocks finished, the elapsed and the remaining time (see "Progress bars and silent" below).

Many FAO series start in 1950 with low catches, which CMSY++ flags as ambiguous (depleted or unexploited) and for which it suggests a start year: the first year with 40% of the maximum catch. `auto_start = TRUE` uses that year (CMSY++'s own `auto.start` stops with an error in `CMSY++16.R`, so the same rule is applied to the start year before the run, and not used if fewer than ten years would remain). The user guide prefers setting `StartYear` or the start B/k prior (`stb.low`, `stb.hi`) yourself.

The example is the 30 stocks with the largest catch in 2015–2024 in FAO area 34 (Eastern Central Atlantic), run with the start years suggested by CMSY++ (`p_green`: probability of the green Kobe quadrant, B ≥ Bmsy and F ≤ Fmsy, in the last year):

```{r}
top30 <- read.csv(file.path(fig_dir, "..", "top30_area34.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
show_table(top30[, c("rank", "Stock", "species_en", "scientific_name", "first_year", "B_Bmsy", "F_Fmsy", "p_green", "status")],
           n = 30, digits = 2)
```

Bigeye grunt (*Brachydeuterus auritus*, `GRB_34`, ninth by catch) is the clearest healthy stock: last-year B/Bmsy 1.42 (95% CI 1.08–1.65), F/Fmsy 0.64, a 93% probability of the green quadrant. It is the example below. Its priors and results tables, from `cmsy_tables()` (Step 9):

```{r}
show_table(read.csv(file.path(fig_dir, "priors_table.csv"), check.names = FALSE))
show_table(read.csv(file.path(fig_dir, "results_table.csv"), check.names = FALSE))
```

`result$summary` has MSY, Bmsy, Fmsy, r and k with their 95% limits, the last-year B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy and biomass with their limits, the probability of each Kobe quadrant and of B/Bmsy below 0.8, the status in two schemes (`status`, FAO; `status_palomares`, Palomares et al. 2018), all priors with their sources and CMSY++'s own notes (such as `suggested_start_year`). `result$series` gives catch, predicted catch, B/k, biomass, B/Bmsy, F and F/Fmsy by year with 95% limits; `result$details` the posterior draws of r, k and B/k and the prior parameters; and `result$sources` the versions and links of CMSY++, JAGS, R, the R packages, the FAO data and FishBase used.

## 📊 Step 6: charts

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cmsy_plot(result, lang = "en")
```

Based on a survey of the charts of 54 CMSY application papers, `cmsy_plot()` draws, for each stock, every chart of the CMSY++ user guide, and the usual summaries of several stocks, in `figures/png/cmsy/<stock>/` and `figures/png/cmsy/summary/` (and as PowerPoint with `pptx = TRUE`).

**By default only axis titles and labels are shown**, so charts can take report captions of their own. Titles, subtitles, captions (method, data and prior sources), legends and text in the charts (quadrant probabilities, PPVR, Mohn's rho) are switched on with `annotations`: `TRUE` for all, or e.g. `c("title", "legend")`; `options(faofishingreport.cmsy_annotations = TRUE)` changes the session default.

| Chart | Content |
|---|---|
| `analysis` | The six panels of the CMSY++ analysis chart (user guide Figure 1): catch and MSY, explored r-k pairs with the prior box, viable r-k pairs, B/k with its three priors, F/Fmsy, equilibrium curve |
| `catch`, `rk`, `biomass`, `b_bmsy`, `exploitation`, `equilibrium` | The same panels as single charts, and B/Bmsy (lines at Bmsy, 0.8 Bmsy, 0.5 Bmsy) |
| `management` | The four management panels (Figure 2): catch and MSY, B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy, Kobe plot |
| `kobe` | Kobe plot (Figure 3): path from the first (square) through the intermediate (circle) to the last year (triangle), 50/80/95% regions of the last-year draws, quadrant probabilities |
| `prior_posterior` | Prior and posterior of r, k, MSY and B/k in three years, with PPVR (Figure 4) |
| `retrospective` | B/Bmsy and F/Fmsy without the last 1–3 years, with Mohn's rho (Figure 5; needs `cmsy_run(plots = "retrospective")`) |
| `overview`, `kobe_all` | Last-year B/Bmsy of each stock with limits; Kobe plot of all stocks (sized by catch) |
| `status`, `status_time`, `histogram` | Share of stocks and of catch by status, in the last year and every year; distribution of last-year B/Bmsy |
| `b_bmsy_all`, `trend`, `aggregate` | Small multiples of B/Bmsy; median B/Bmsy and share below 0.8 Bmsy; total catch / total MSY and total biomass / total Bmsy |
| `map` | Median last-year B/Bmsy by FAO fishing area |

Status follows FAO (2026) for Tier 3 (data-limited) assessments by default: maximally sustainably fished (B/Bmsy ≥ 0.8) or overfished. `classes = "palomares"` uses the five classes of Palomares et al. (2018), common in CMSY studies: healthy (≥ 1), slightly overfished (0.8–1), overfished (0.5–0.8), grossly overfished (0.2–0.5), collapsed (< 0.2).

The CMSY++ analysis chart of bigeye grunt (no annotations, the default):

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_analysis.png")
```

Management chart:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_management.png")
```

Kobe plot with `annotations = TRUE`:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_kobe.png")
```

Prior and posterior distributions; the smaller the PPVR, the more the data added to the prior:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_prior_posterior.png")
```

Retrospective analysis:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_retrospective.png")
```

Summaries of the 30 stocks of area 34 (`annotations = "legend"`):

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("area34_overview.png")
show_png("area34_kobe_all.png")
show_png("area34_status_time.png")
show_png("area34_map.png")
```

## 🔮 Step 7: projections under fishing scenarios

```{r, eval = FALSE}
projection <- cmsy_forecast(result, catch = 100000)
```

`CMSY++16.R` has no projection, so `cmsy_forecast()` projects with the CMSY++ model itself (Schaefer surplus production with productivity declining below 0.25 k), from the posterior draws of r, k and last-year B/k of the same MCMC iterations, with lognormal process error (`sigma`, 0.1 by default as `sigmaR` in CMSY++). The default scenarios are 0.5, 0.6, 0.8 and 0.95 Fmsy (as in Froese et al. 2018) and the last-year fishing mortality; constant catches can be added (`catch`). It gives B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy and catch by year with 95% limits, the probability that B is at least Bmsy and, for several stocks, the share of stocks at or above Bmsy.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_forecast.png")
```

## 🔍 Step 8: compare runs or other assessments

```{r, eval = FALSE}
result_1950 <- cmsy_run(input, stocks = "GRB_34", seed = 1)        # starting in 1950
cmsy_compare(`1950` = result_1950, `CMSY++` = result, stocks = "GRB_34")
```

`cmsy_compare()` draws several runs (e.g. different start years or priors, a sensitivity analysis) and other estimates (`external`, e.g. B/Bmsy from ICES, JABBA or a paper) together and lists their last-year values. Started in 1950, bigeye grunt has a last-year B/Bmsy of 1.14; started in 1978 as CMSY++ suggests, 1.42; both are above Bmsy:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show_png("grunt_compare.png")
```

## 📋 Step 9: tables for reports

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tables <- cmsy_tables(result, lang = "en")
```

`cmsy_tables()` makes the two tables of CMSY papers, the priors table and the results table shown in Step 5, rounded, with ranges as "low-high" and column names in the chosen language, saved in `tables/cmsy/`.

## ⚙️ The settings of CMSY++

CMSY++ has a set of general settings, such as the catch observation error `CV.C`, the process error `sigmaR` and the number of MCMC chains and iterations. `cmsy_run()` keeps the CMSY++ values unless they are changed; `cmsy_defaults()` lists each one with its CMSY++ default, the value used and what it does:

```{r}
show_table(cmsy_defaults(lang = "en")[, c("setting", "cmsy_default", "applies_to", "description")], n = 30)
```

Settings marked "BSM" only matter with abundance data (CPUE or biomass); with FAO catch data only those marked "all" affect the results. To change some, give only those in `settings`; the others keep their CMSY++ values, and every value is checked (name, range, enough MCMC draws):

```{r}
cmsy_defaults(list(sigmaR = 0.15, n.iter = 100000, n.burnin = 50000))[c(3, 17, 18), c("setting", "cmsy_default", "used", "changed")]
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
result <- cmsy_run(input, stocks = "GRB_34", seed = 1, auto_start = TRUE,
                   settings = list(sigmaR = 0.15, n.iter = 100000, n.burnin = 50000))
result$settings[result$settings$changed, ]          # the changed settings
```

The settings used are saved in `settings_used.csv` of the run folder and recorded in `result$sources`. The chart and output switches of CMSY++ (`mgraphs`, `kobe.plot`, `retros`, ...) are set by the `plots` argument of `cmsy_run()`, not in `settings`.

## 🖥️ Windows, macOS and Linux

The same code runs on all three systems: `cmsy_system()` detects the system and makes the changes it needs (on macOS, no `windows()` and no `antialias = "cleartype"`; see Step 1), and the JAGS installer is chosen for the system and R version. Each change to the CMSY code is checked by the GitHub Actions workflow "CMSY-cross-platform" on Windows, macOS and Linux: it downloads and installs JAGS with `cmsy_install_jags()`, runs CMSY++ for real, runs all CMSY tests and keeps the output of each system.

## ⏱️ Progress bars and silent

`cmsy_run()`, `cmsy_plot()`, `cmsy_forecast()` and `cmsy_area()` show progress bars such as

```
CMSY++ [==================            ] 18/30 ( 60%) 00:51 elapsed, 00:34 left GAL_34
```

All CMSY functions have a `silent` argument: with `silent = TRUE` they print no progress bars or messages (`cmsy_setup()` still asks before installing). `fao_settings(silent = TRUE)` sets the session default.
